snapshot.title: UPSC Environment: Pollution Rules & CRZ
snapshot.exam_hook: ⚡ UPSC v12.0 Hook: 120 microns: Plastic. 8 pollutants: AQI (No CO2). CRZ-I: Sensitive. EPR: Producer responsibility.

quick_notes.title: Plastic Waste Rules (2016/2021)
quick_notes.detail: Banned Single-Use Plastic (SUP) from July 2022. Thickness : 120 microns (as of Dec 2022). EPR is mandatory for producers.
quick_notes.explanation: Plastic Waste Rules (2016/2021) are government regulations that aim to reduce plastic pollution. These rules banned single-use plastic (SUP), which means disposable plastic items used only once, starting from July 2022. As of December 2022, the rules require plastic carry bags and sheets to have a minimum thickness of 120 microns, where a micron is one-millionth of a meter, so that the plastic is stronger and easier to recycle

quick_notes.title: E-Waste Rules (2022)
quick_notes.detail: Covers solar panels now. Trading in EPR certificates allowed. Targets for recycling are fixed.
quick_notes.explanation: The E-Waste (Management) Rules, 2022 are Indian government regulations that control how electronic waste, or e-waste, is handled. E-waste means discarded electrical or electronic items like old phones, computers, and now also solar panels, which are included for the first time under these rules. EPR stands for Extended Producer Responsibility, which is a system where the company that makes a product is responsible for collecting and recycling it after use. Under these rules, companies can now trade EPR certificates, meaning one company can buy or sell the credit it earns for meeting its recycling target to another company. The rules also set fixed recycling targets, which are specific percentages of e-waste that producers must collect and recycle each year.

quick_notes.title: Hazardous Waste Rules
quick_notes.detail: Focus on "Transboundary movement" (Basel Convention). Import of waste for disposal is prohibited.
quick_notes.explanation: Hazardous waste is any waste that is dangerous to human health or the environment, such as chemicals or medical waste. The Basel Convention is an international treaty that controls the transboundary movement of hazardous waste, which means the shipping of such waste from one country to another. Under India's Hazardous and Other Wastes (Management and Transboundary Movement) Rules, which implement the Basel Convention, importing hazardous waste for the purpose of disposal is completely prohibited. However, importing such waste for recycling or reuse may be allowed under strict conditions and with government permission. This rule helps prevent countries from dumping dangerous waste in nations that lack the facilities to manage it safely.

quick_notes.title: CRZ (Coastal Regulation Zone)
quick_notes.detail: CRZ-I (Ecologically sensitive), CRZ-II (Urban built-up), CRZ-III (Rural), CRZ-IV (Water area). No-Development Zone (NDZ) is 20m for islands.
quick_notes.explanation: CRZ stands for Coastal Regulation Zone, which are rules made by the Indian government to protect the coastline and control what can be built near the sea. The coast is divided into four categories: CRZ-I covers ecologically sensitive areas like mangroves and coral reefs where almost no construction is allowed; CRZ-II covers urban areas that are already built-up, like cities, where some construction is allowed with restrictions; CRZ-III covers rural and undeveloped coastal areas where building is limited; and CRZ-IV covers the water area itself, including the sea and tidal waters. A No-Development Zone (NDZ) is a strip of land along the coast where no new buildings are permitted, and for islands, this strip is 20 meters wide from the high tide line. These rules aim to balance development with protecting the fragile coastal environment for future generations.

quick_notes.title: AQI (Air Quality Index)
quick_notes.detail: 8 pollutants: PM10, PM2.5, NO2, SO2, CO, O3, NH3, Pb. Launched in 2014 ("One Color, One Description").
quick_notes.explanation: The Air Quality Index or AQI is a simple number that tells you how clean or polluted the air in your area is. It was launched in 2014 with the idea of "One Color, One Description", meaning that across India the same color (for example, green for good) will always mean the same level of health risk. The AQI is calculated using eight different pollutants: PM10 (coarse dust particles smaller than 10 micrometers), PM2.5 (fine dust particles smaller than 2.5 micrometers that can enter your lungs), NO2 (nitrogen dioxide, a gas from vehicles), SO2 (sulfur dioxide, from burning coal), CO (carbon monoxide, a poisonous gas), O3 (ozone, a gas that can irritate your lungs), NH3 (ammonia, often from farming), and Pb (lead, a heavy metal from old fuel or industry). Each of these pollutants is measured, and the worst one determines the overall AQI number and color for that day.
